title: The shtetl
hookLine: the small market towns of Eastern Europe

cards: Market day. Carts roll in from the villages before dawn: peasants with eggs, grain, a cow to sell.
In the square, Jewish shopkeepers open their stalls and the bargaining starts, in Yiddish, in Polish, in Ukrainian, in whatever works. The street is mud in spring and dust in summer.

Somewhere a tailor is at work, a water carrier sloshes past with two buckets, and from an open window comes the sing-song of boys reading Torah aloud. Today, the place where all of this happened at once.

teach.b: Shtetl is the Yiddish word for a small town. It names the market towns of Eastern Europe, in the lands of Poland and beyond, where Jewish families lived beside Christian neighbors who came in to trade.
A shtetl had a shape. The market square at its center.
The synagogue, and next to it the study house, where men and boys read and argued over the Talmud. The mikveh, the ritual bath. The cemetery at the edge of town.
Around them, wooden houses and the trades that kept everyone fed: tailors, cobblers, innkeepers, peddlers, teachers.
Life was hard. Families were often poor, fires could take a street in a night, and a ruler's whim or a riot could turn everything over. But the week had a rhythm stronger than any of that.
On Friday afternoon the shops closed, the bathhouse filled, the bread was baked, and when the candles were lit Shabbat came in, and for a day even the poorest home could feel like a palace.

Writers in Yiddish loved the shtetl and teased it at the same time. Sholem Aleichem invented a town called Kasrilevke, poor and crowded and full of characters, and wrote about it with laughter and tenderness.
Today we have the word, the stories and the photographs. What happened to the towns themselves, we will come to later in the year.

how: Some Ashkenazi Jewish families trace their roots to a particular shtetl, and some keep memorial books (yizkor books) that record its streets, families and customs.

games.q: it's Friday afternoon in the shtetl. the week was hard and money is short. what happens next?
o: shops stay open late to make up the money.
shops close, bread is baked, and candles bring in Shabbat.
everyone goes to the market in the next town.
games.why: the week's rhythm was stronger than the hardship: Shabbat came in, and even a poor home could feel like a palace.

practice: It's Friday afternoon on a shtetl street: feel the mud under your boots, smell bread baking, hear a shopkeeper pulling down a shutter.
Now the light is going, and in window after window a candle is lit; walk down that street slowly, and let it be quiet.

wordCard.voice: Shtetl. A small market town of Eastern Europe, Jewish at its heart: a square, a synagogue, a study house, mud, poverty and Shabbat candles. Today's word.
